summary: Defines a MIB module for managing printer finishing subunits, devices attached to a printer system that do things like staple. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is the dashboard for the machine attached to a printer that staples or sorts the pages.

how does snmp manage printer stapling
subtitle: An SNMP MIB for managing the stapling, folding, punching and binding units attached to a printer.

tldr.problem: Network printers and copiers increasingly include in-line finishing such as stapling, folding and punching, but the Printer MIB gave no well-defined way to monitor or configure those finisher units.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Finisher MIB, an extension of the Printer MIB, with tables for finisher devices, supplies, media inputs and an enum-keyed attribute table, plus a companion IANA-maintained MIB for extensible enumerations.
tldr.outcome: Management applications can read finisher status and capabilities, enable or disable finishing processes and see which combinations are invalid. The RFC is informational.

today: RFC 3806 is an Informational RFC and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it. It extends the Printer MIB, RFC 3805.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The Printer Finishing MIB is an SNMP Management Information Base for in-line post-processing of printed pages. It extends the Printer MIB (RFC 3805), and the authors expect it to be folded into a future Printer MIB update. It can provide the status of the finishing device, query and control its features and configuration, enable and disable finishing processes, and allow unsolicited status from the device.

The scope is deliberately rich, because finishing normally goes with higher-speed network printers and copiers. It does not duplicate production mail preparation, custom insertion, franking and reprints, which the DMTF Large Mailing Operations standard covers. Information from the MIB can serve monitoring tools and job submission tools working at print-job level or document level. Compatible combinations of processes are implementation specific, and the MIB lets invalid combinations be identified.
sections.eli5: It lets a computer ask the stapler-and-folder box beside a printer what it can do and whether it is working.

sections.title: Finishing Vocabulary and Geometry
sections.content:
The MIB borrows its terms from the ISO Document Printing Application (DPA), the DMTF Large Mailing Operations standard and the Internet Printing Protocol. A finishing process is an operation such as trimming, folding or binding. A finishing specification is an ordered combination of processes, and order matters: folding then trimming gives a different result from trimming then folding.

Positions are described with a Reference Edge, a Finishing Process Axis parallel to it, a Finishing Process Offset between them, and Head Locations along the axis. Everything is defined relative to a portrait view of the medium, with the X axis along the short edge. The RFC also defines process terms for folding (Z fold, half fold, letter fold), binding, trimming, stapling and stitching, wrapping, banding and sheet rotation.
sections.eli5: To tell a stapler where to staple, you need words like "which edge" and "how far in". This part defines those words so everyone means the same thing.

sections.title: Where Finishers Fit in the Printer Model
sections.content:
Finisher subunits receive media from one or more Printer Media Path subunits and deliver it to one or more Printer Output subunits after finishing. The RFC modifies the Printer MIB model by adding finisher subunits and finisher supplies between the media path and the outputs.

Each finishing operation the printer supports is represented by one or more entries in the finDeviceTable. Each entry is a logical finishing device, since one mechanism may serve several entries and several mechanisms may do the same job. A hole punch that makes several holes may need an entry per hole position, or per head mechanism if heads differ in pattern or size.
sections.eli5: The finisher sits between the printer and the output tray, like a station on a conveyor belt that staples pages before they land in the tray.

sections.title: The Attribute Mechanism
sections.content:
Rather than a new object for every capability, the MIB uses attributes identified by an enum instead of an OID. New attributes can be registered without changing the MIB, and a device that lacks a feature simply omits the attribute. Attributes live in a four-indexed finDeviceAttributeTable, indexed by hrDeviceIndex, finDeviceIndex, the attribute type and the attribute instance.

An agent SHALL implement an attribute if the device supports the function and the information is available, and SHOULD NOT create the row otherwise. Each row has both an integer value and an octet-string value; the unused one returns a zero-length string or -1. When no useful value exists, the agent returns a zero-length string, unknown(2) for enums, 0 for indexes and -2 for counts. Attributes marked MULTI-ROW may occur several times per subunit.

Examples include maximumSheets, finReferenceEdge, finAxisOffset, finHeadLocation and finOperationRestrictions, which names finishing processes that cannot be combined. Type-specific groups cover stitchers, folders, binders, trimmers, die cutters and punchers. Punch patterns carry implied defaults, for example two-hole US top punching with hole spacing of 2.75 inches.
sections.eli5: Instead of a separate switch for every possible feature, the machine keeps a list of labelled notes. It only writes a note if it actually has that feature.

sections.title: Enumerations and the IANA MIB
sections.content:
Enumerations are symbolic value sets, defined as textual conventions. The RFC uses two categories. In Type 1, all legal values are in the Finisher MIB, and new values need a new Finisher MIB document. In Type 2, values are registered in the companion IANA Finisher MIB, and new values need Designated Expert Review. Attribute enum values from 2^30 to 2^31-1 are reserved for private or experimental use.

Some Integer32 objects also use the special values other(-1), unknown(-2) and partial(-3), where partial means some supply or capacity remains but the amount is unknown. IANA is to archive the initial IANA Finisher MIB and maintain it under the process in the RFC.
sections.eli5: Some lists of names are locked in the book. Others are kept by a librarian who adds new names when an expert says okay.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access, such as finDevicePresentOnOff, capacities and media input dimensions, may be sensitive. The RFC rates the possible harm from writes as minor or severe inconvenience, with finDevicePresentOnOff and the media input dimension objects rated severe. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security, so the RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Vendors may implement read-write objects as read-only, for example when the device senses the value itself.
sections.eli5: If anyone could change the stapler's settings from afar, they could cause trouble. So only trusted people should be allowed, with proper locks.
